stories.title: Overview of Crop Monitoring
stories.description: An overview of different tools coming from ESA that can support crop monitoring in Europe.

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
Croplands are widespread across Europe, covering almost a quarter (22.5%) of EU territory. 

This image shows a map of land cover across Europe (from the ESA [WorldCover](https://esa-worldcover.org/en) project), with croplands shown in purple.

content.title: CLMS HRL Cropland
content.description:
The [High Resolution Layer Croplands](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/high-resolution-layer-croplands) products are produced by the [Copernicus Land Monitoring Service](https://land.copernicus.eu/en). 

These products show crop types and cropping patterns at 10m resolution, produced annually but with some ywars delay.

They are mainly intended for use by researchers, policymakers, farmers and other stakeholders interested in analysing the European agricultural landscape.

This image shows a sample of the CLMS Crop Type product in the south of Germany.

content.title: Sen4CAP algorithms
content.description:
The ESA Funded [Sen4CAP](https://www.esa-sen4cap.org) (Sentinels for the Common Agricultural Policy) project has produced a set of toolboxes that can be used to provide key information in support of CAP Monitoring.

This includes determining key spectral indices and biophysical parameters, as well as crop type maps and informaton on agricultural practices.

The Sen4CAP algorithms are now available to run online through ESA's [APEX algorithm catalogue](https://algorithm-catalogue.apex.esa.int/?q=Sen4CAP).

This image shows a crop type map produced through Sen4CAP for three years in the area around Prague. You can zoom in or

content.title: The WorldCereal System
content.description:
The [WorldCereal](https://esa-worldcereal.org/en) project has produced a set of toolboxes that can be used to provide key information in support of CAP Monitoring.

The [WorldCereal toolbox](https://esa-worldcereal.org/en/products/worldcereal-system) has been designed to support the cost-efficient production of land cover and crop type maps at local to global scales, though for a more limited range of crop types than Sen4CAP.

This toolbox is also available through ESA's [APEx initiative](https://algorithm-catalogue.apex.esa.int/?q=WorldCereal).

This image shows a crop type map for the UK in 2022 produced using the WorldCereal toolbox.

content.title: Automated Parcel Mapping
content.description:
Artificial Intelligence models can be used to automate the determine field boundaries based on Sentinel data. The ESA-funded [Delineate Anything](https://lavreniuk.github.io/Delineate-Anything/) project has done tests in a wide number of European countries.

This image shows an example in Italy's Po valley, with a Sentinel image as a background. Use the navigation tools to look at different areas.

content.title: AI for Tillage Monitoring
content.description:
AI models can also be used for other purposes. The ESA [AI for Tillage](https://eo4society.esa.int/projects/ai-based-tillage-detection-for-improved-agricultural-and-climate-policies) project has used such models to detect tillage events. 

It can also determine the type of tillage used: **Conventional tillage**,  known for its intensive soil disturbance, or **Conservation tillage** which maintains permanent or semi-permanent soil coverage, thereby promoting soil health and minimizing erosion. 

On the right we see assessment of tillage for selected parcels in Estonia. Click on a parcel to see the estimated date of each tillage event and whether it was performed using conventional or conservation methods, as well as an assessment of the confidence.

content.title: Carbon Farming
content.description: This images shows a high resolution map of soil organic carbon, as developed under the ESA-Funded [EO for Carbon Farming](https://business.esa.int/projects/eo4carbonfarming) project.

content.title: Conclusion
content.description:
The ESA Stakeholder Requirements Facility helps to build connections between available products and user requirements

For more information on available tools and services, see the [SEF Food Systems page](https://sef.apex.esa.int/en/key-themes/food-systems).

If you are a potential user of such services we would like to know more about your needs and the gaps with respect to existing capabilities. Please [contact us](https://sef.apex.esa.int/en/contact-us) to discuss more.

If you are a data provider who is interested in having yuor products included in this demo, then we would be interested in discussing more.

stories.title: Crop Mapping in England
stories.description: An example of using the WorldCereal system to map crops in the UK

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
[WorldCereal](https://esa-worldcereal.org/en) is a research project funded by the European Space Agency, aimed at providing a free, cloud-based processing system to generate high-resolution custom crop location and type products at local and global scales.

The WorldCereal consortium has provided detailed and seasonally updated global maps of temporary crops, crop type (maize, winter cereals and spring cereals) and irrigation, with examples available for the 2021 reference year.

The project also offers a cloud-based processing system allowing anyone to train and apply cropland/crop type detection models using open EO datasets.

content.title: Presto embedding
content.description:
The WorldCereal system uses a set of [presto embeddings](https://nasaharvest.github.io/presto-embeddings/) to encode multi-modal satellite data (Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, meteorological data, DEM, and location) at a 10-meter pixel scale into.

From this, further information about the different types of crops can be extracted.

content.title: Local Monitoring
content.description: To showcase the level of detail available we zoom into a smaller region in East Anglia, one of the most productive crop regions in the UK.

content.title: Field Delineation
content.description: Artificial Intelligence models from the ESA-funded [Delineate Anything](https://lavreniuk.github.io/Delineate-Anything/) project can be used to determine field boundaries.

content.title: Spring Cereals
content.description:
WorldCereal provides several season-specific products, generated at the end of a growing season. 

This example shows the fields in which spring cereals have been detected (in brown) for the 2021 reference year.

content.title: Winter Cereals
content.description: This can be compared to field in which winter cereals have been detected (in brown), also for the 2021 reference year.

content.title: Crop Type Mapping
content.description:
As well as the systematically generated products shown previously, WorldCereal also provides more detailed crop mapping using an [on-demand system](https://esa-worldcereal.org/en/products/worldcereal-system). 

This example was performed for the GTIF Uk project, and was processed using Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, Copernicus DEM and AgERA5 meteo data from 2021-10-01 till 2022-09-30 using a customized finetuning of the WorldCereal seasonal model suite using the available data over UK and Western Europe.

content.title: Crop Type Mapping (UK wide)
content.description: This on-demand system can be applied to wider areas, as shown by this UK-wide map.

content.title: Worldwide products
content.description:
The WorldCereal systems can also be used to detect growth of key crops worldwide.

This image shows worldwide the production of Maize for the 2021 reference year.

content.title: Further Information
content.description:
For more information visit the [WorldCereal](https://esa-worldcereal.org/en) website.

Field delineation was performed using outputs from the [Delineate Anything](https://lavreniuk.github.io/Delineate-Anything/) project.

stories.title: Tillage Montoring in Estonia
stories.description: Using AI models to detect different tillage methods.

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
As part of its [CAP strategic plan](https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/cap-my-country/cap-strategic-plans/estonia_en) Estonia is devoting a large part of its total CAP budget to support environmental and climate objectives, including carbon sequestration.

There are several ways in which agricultural practices can be changed to improve carbon sequestration. This story looks in particular at tillage practices.

It is based on work performed by [KappaZeta](www.kappazeta.ee) under the [ESA-funded AI for Tillage Detection](https://eo4society.esa.int/projects/ai-based-tillage-detection-for-improved-agricultural-and-climate-policies/) project.

content.title: Farming In Estonia
content.description:
Approximately 15% (6627 square km) of Estonia is devoted to cropland. 

This image shows the different types of crops grown in the region where the AI for tillage study was performed. 

Data from [CLMS HRL Cropland](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/high-resolution-layer-croplands) for 2017.

content.title: Crop Monitoring
content.description:
This image shows two of the many ways in which we can use Sentinel data to monitor changes. On the left is an image in the near infrared (NIR), on the right the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI).

There are many other possible ways of analysing images, and by looking at how these change over time (over a sequence of satellite images) we can what sort of changes occur and when they happen.

Images from WorldCover via Terrascope.

content.title: Tillage Monitoring
content.description:
One such change that we can look for is when a farmer turns the soil to prepare the land for farming, a practice known as **tillage**. 

![Tractor ploughing](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/12/Cultivating_near_Barton_Hill_Farm_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1994147.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)


*Image by David Wright, CC BY-SA 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=17504116.*

content.title: Types of Tillage
content.description:
The more intense the tillage, the more the carbon stored in the soil is released into the atmosphere. 

**Conventional tillage** is known for its intensive soil disturbance, which can negatively impact biodiversity, disrupt soil nutrient balance, and increase GHG emissions. 

**Conservation tillage** is a method that maintains permanent or semi-permanent soil coverage, thereby promoting soil health and minimizing erosion. Practices under this category, such as [no-tillage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-till_farming), [mulch tillage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulch-till), and [ridge tillage](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/ridge-tillage), aim to enhance soil conservation and improve crop yields.

content.title: Detecting tillage through AI
content.description:
These differences in tillage can be detected from Sentinel data, and an AI model has been trained to assess them.

On the right we see assessment of tillage for selected parcels. Click on a parcel to see the estimated date of each tillage event and whether it was performed using conventional or conservation methods, as well as an assessment of the confidence.

content.title: Further Reading
content.description:
Kappazeta have written more about their work on this project in [a blog post on their website](https://kappazeta.ee/blog/detecting-tillage-intensity-from-space/) and [this article on medium](https://medium.com/kappazeta/farming-footprints-mapping-tillage-practices-with-earth-observation-and-ai-dc43cac86e83).

**Acknowledgements:**

Tillage analysis provided by [Kappazeta](https://kappazeta.ee/) and available in the [APEx PRR](https://browser.apex.esa.int/external/eoresults.esa.int/stac/collections/tillage_type_detection).

Crop maps from CLMS HRL Croplands.

stories.title: Carbon Farming in Bavaria
stories.description: An overview of different EO based services for monitoring Carbon Farming.

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
[Carbon Farming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_farming) is a set of agricultural practices that aim to increase the retention of carbon in biomass and soil. Within Europe the new [CRCF regulation](https://climate.ec.europa.eu/areas-action/carbon-removals-and-carbon-farming/carbon-removals-and-carbon-farming-crcf-regulation_en) is expected to lead to an increased use of carbon farming practices.

Earth observation based solutions have a strong potential to support the monitoring and verification of carbon farming.

This story showcases several such produces which have been developed under the ESA-Funded [EO for Carbon Farming](https://business.esa.int/projects/eo4carbonfarming) project.

content.title: Crop Monitoring
content.description:
Satellites are already widely used in crop mapping, determining which crops have been planted in individual fields.

This layer shows an extract from the [HRL Cropland](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/high-resolution-layer-croplands) service provided by CLMS:

content.title: Verification of crop rotation
content.description:
One basic practice for carbon retention is simply to ensure adequate crop rotation. 

This layer uses Sentinel data to assess adherence to crop rotation rules over several growing seasons.

Fields outlined in green have a valid crop rotation, whereas fields visualised in red dont show the crop rotation indicated by the customer. Fields with a wrong crop type in just one year are visualised in yellow.

content.title: Catch crop development
content.description:
[Catch crops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catch_crop) are grown between two successive plantings of the main crop, enhancing soil biology and hence carbon retention.

In this layer NDVI and biomass estimation from Sentinel data are to monitor the development of catch crops in selected fields over time. Such data can be used to assess if planting is being done in compliance to the declaration.

Use the time scroller to see the evolution of the catch crop.

content.title: Catch crop planting detection
content.description:
Usiong such techniques, the services can detect layer catch crop planting without any information from the customer other than the field boundaries. 

Fields visualized in green are verified as fields with catch crops, whereas fields visualized in brown are classified as fields without catch crops. Uncertain fields are coloured in ochre.

content.title: Soil Organic Carbon
content.description:
Selected earth observation data can be combined with in-situ data to provide a detailed assessment of Soil Organic Carbon.

This image shows high resolution Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) for a selected area of Bavaria in 2017.

content.title: Soil Organic Carbon (parcel level)
content.description: Given field boundaries, these measurements can be used to assess the SOC content of a particular field.

content.title: Soil Organic Carbon (relative)
content.description: This images shows the relative SOC at field level, showing those areas (red) with higher SOC content and those (blue) with lower than expected SOC.

content.title: Stratification
content.description: This map shows the spatially continuous relative SOC content in a 10x10m raster including a zone map with homogeneous soil zones by using a Sentinel-2 time series. It is used to stratify the soil sampling, which is required for several certification standards.

content.title: Overall carbon binding
content.description: Assessment of overall carbon binding in soil and biomass (OCB). This layer shows how much carbon is bound in biomass to complement information about carbon stored in soils. The algorithm combines S2 time series with physical crop growth modelling driven by meteorological data as well as the SOC content and crop rotation on the field.

content.title: Further Information
content.description:
For more information see the [EO4Carbon Farming](https://business.esa.int/projects/eo4carbonfarming) project page.

For background on carbon farming see the [CRCF regulation](https://climate.ec.europa.eu/areas-action/carbon-removals-and-carbon-farming/carbon-removals-and-carbon-farming-crcf-regulation_en).

This interactive map shows field boundaries across all major European Countries generated using the **Delineate Anything v2** algorithm applied to the 2025 summer season Sentinel-2 Global Mosaics (S2GM), with the WorldCereal 2021 map used as a delineation mask.

 To view the field boundaries, zoom in to a local in a country of your choice. The boundaries are displayed on the map when the scalebar in the bottom left displays 5 km or less.

**Please note** that the field boundaries are overlaid on high-resolution satellite imagery from the Stadia Maps service. As a result, some misalignment may be visible, since the boundaries were derived from Sentinel-2 data.

### Further information
Details of methodology are available on the [Delineate Anything Project Page](https://lavreniuk.github.io/Delineate-Anything/)

‘Water Stress and Climate Indices for Africa’ (WaSCIA) was an ESA funded project that aims to deliver high-quality Water Stress and Climate Indices through an easy-to-use web interface to help the management of drought and water stress in Africa. The project started in 2022 and ended in 2024. The project was led by Telespazio UK in collaboration with RSS Hydro, Telespazio UK and three Stakeholders, Centre Régional de Formation et d'Application en Agrométéorologie et Hydrologie Opérationnelle (AGRHYMET), Laboratoire Physique de l'Atmosphère et de l'Océan Simeon Fongang (LPAOSF) and Direction de la Gestion et de la Planification des Ressources en Eau (DGPRE).
The main outputs from WaSCIA were:
- Climate Indices. Telespazio UK developed an application (wascia_processor_climate_indicators) that allows the generation of 20 climate indices. In addition, a set of Jupyter Notebooks were also developed for the flexible and interactive analysis of the climate data, enabling end-users to quickly assess the climate condition in their region of interest and analyse both the long-term trends in climate variability and the current season anomalies up to 5 days behind real time. The end-users can interrogate the data and produce customised metrics useful for their operations. The WASCIA results are limited to the area of Senegal.
- Soil Moisture Indices

‘Water Stress and Climate Indices for Africa’ (WaSCIA) was an ESA funded project that aims to deliver high-quality Water Stress and Climate Indices through an easy-to-use web interface to help the management of drought and water stress in Africa. The project started in 2022 and ended in 2024. The project was led by Telespazio UK in collaboration with RSS Hydro, Telespazio UK and three Stakeholders, Centre Régional de Formation et d'Application en Agrométéorologie et Hydrologie Opérationnelle (AGRHYMET), Laboratoire Physique de l'Atmosphère et de l'Océan Simeon Fongang (LPAOSF) and Direction de la Gestion et de la Planification des Ressources en Eau (DGPRE).
The main outputs from WaSCIA were:
- Climate Indices. Telespazio UK developed an application (wascia_processor_climate_indicators) that allows the generation of 20 climate indices. In addition, a set of Jupyter Notebooks were also developed for the flexible and interactive analysis of the climate data, enabling end-users to quickly assess the climate condition in their region of interest and analyse both the long-term trends in climate variability and the current season anomalies up to 5 days behind real time. The end-users can interrogate the data and produce customised metrics useful for their operations. The WASCIA results are limited to the area of Senegal.
- Soil Moisture Indices
